assessments.explanation: HMC's momentum-and-gradient leapfrog trajectory produces large, directed proposals that stay likely to be accepted because they follow the shape of the posterior. The samples are much less autocorrelated than from an undirected random-walk step at a comparable acceptance rate, so HMC scales much better to the high-dimensional models these libraries target. The “HMC eliminates the need for a burn-in…” option is false: HMC still needs a warm-up or burn-in phase like any MCMC method. The “HMC works by computing the marginal likelihood…” option is false: no MCMC method here needs the marginal likelihood. The “HMC only requires evaluating the posterior…” option is false: the leapfrog trajectory evaluates the gradient at many intermediate points per proposal, so each step costs more evaluations than plain Metropolis-Hastings, not fewer.

assessments.prompt: Explain to a colleague how Metropolis-Hastings, Gibbs sampling, and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo each let you sample from a posterior without ever computing the marginal likelihood, and what distinguishes the three from each other.
assessments.modelAnswer: All three methods share the same foundational trick: they need only RATIOS of the unnormalized posterior (likelihood times prior) evaluated at two points, and the marginal likelihood, a single constant that multiplies the normalized posterior at every point equally, cancels out of any such ratio. None of them computes the intractable evidence integral from earlier in this module; they sidestep it. Metropolis-Hastings is the general-purpose version: at each step it proposes a new state from some proposal distribution and accepts it with probability equal to the minimum of 1 and the ratio of unnormalized posterior densities (adjusted for proposal asymmetry, if any), so it can be applied to essentially any target you can evaluate, at the cost of possibly slow, highly autocorrelated exploration if the proposal is a poor match for the target's shape. Gibbs sampling specializes this idea for cases where each variable's full conditional distribution, given all the others, happens to be directly tractable to sample from -- using that conditional as the proposal makes the acceptance probability equal 1 every time, so it never wastes a step on rejection, but it requires those tractable conditionals to exist in the first place. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo generalizes random-walk Metropolis-Hastings by using the gradient of the log posterior to simulate a physics-inspired trajectory (via a leapfrog integrator) that proposes a large, directed move which still tends to land in high-density territory, giving much lower autocorrelation between consecutive samples than an undirected random walk, especially in high dimensions. That is why HMC, in its auto-tuned NUTS form, is the default sampler inside modern probabilistic programming tools like Stan, PyMC, and NumPyro.

concepts.title: Variational Inference and the Evidence Lower Bound
concepts.description: Variational inference replaces sampling with optimization: it picks the member of a tractable distributional family closest to the true posterior by maximizing the ELBO, a quantity that decomposes into a reconstruction term minus a KL-divergence-to-the-prior term. That decomposition is the loss function a Variational Autoencoder is trained to maximize.
learningObjectives: Explain the core idea of variational inference: approximating an intractable posterior with the closest member of a tractable distributional family, found by optimization rather than sampling.
Derive the ELBO from the log marginal likelihood using Jensen's inequality, and explain why it is a lower bound.
Decompose the ELBO into an expected-log-likelihood ('reconstruction') term minus a KL-divergence-to-the-prior term, and explain what each term rewards or penalizes.
Explain why maximizing the ELBO over the variational family is exactly equivalent to minimizing the KL divergence between the approximate and true posterior.
State that maximizing this reconstruction-minus-KL objective is what training a Variational Autoencoder means, identifying which network computes which term.

sections.heading: Turning Inference Into Optimization
sections.body:
The previous concept's MCMC methods are asymptotically exact: given enough samples and time, they converge to the true posterior with no built-in bias. That guarantee has a cost. Sampling can be slow to converge, autocorrelation makes it hard to know how many *effectively independent* samples you have, and scaling MCMC to very large datasets or very high-dimensional models (the regime most modern machine learning lives in) is often impractical. **Variational inference (VI)** takes a different approach. Instead of sampling, it picks a family of simple, tractable distributions q(theta; phi), indexed by **variational parameters** phi (for a factorized Gaussian family, a mean and variance per dimension; this choice is called **mean-field** VI), and searches for the member of that family *closest* to the true posterior p(theta | D).

'Closest' needs a definition, and VI's standard choice is the **Kullback-Leibler divergence**, KL(q(theta) || p(theta | D)), a non-negative measure of how far one distribution is from another, equal to 0 only when q and p are identical. The obvious plan, minimizing this KL directly over phi, hits the same wall as the rest of this module: p(theta | D) contains the intractable evidence P(D) in its denominator, so you can't evaluate the quantity you want to minimize, let alone differentiate it. VI's trick is to find a *different* quantity, the ELBO derived next, that you can compute and optimize and that corresponds to minimizing the same intractable KL divergence without touching it.

sections.heading: Deriving the ELBO via Jensen's Inequality
sections.body:
Start from the log marginal likelihood, log P(D), and introduce the variational distribution q(theta) by multiplying and dividing by it inside the integral that defines P(D):

```text
log P(D) = log ∫ P(D, theta) d theta
         = log ∫ q(theta) * [P(D, theta) / q(theta)] d theta
         = log E_q[ P(D, theta) / q(theta) ]
```

That last line rewrites the integral as an expectation under q of the ratio P(D,theta)/q(theta). Now apply **Jensen's inequality**: because log is a concave function, the log of an expectation is always greater than or equal to the expectation of the log, log E[X] >= E[log X], for any positive random variable X. Applying that here:

```text
log P(D) = log E_q[ P(D, theta) / q(theta) ]
         >= E_q[ log( P(D, theta) / q(theta) ) ]
         =  E_q[ log P(D, theta) ] - E_q[ log q(theta) ]
         =: ELBO(q)
```

That right-hand side is the **Evidence Lower BOund**, ELBO(q) -- named for what the inequality just proved: it is a lower bound on the log evidence, log P(D). Every term in ELBO(q) is computable. P(D, theta) is likelihood times prior (the unnormalized posterior you've been evaluating throughout this module), and the expectation is taken under q, the tractable distribution you chose and can sample from freely.

The derivation is more than a loose inequality, because an exact identity governs the gap. Start from P(D, theta) = p(theta | D) * P(D) (the definition of conditional probability, rearranged),

```text
ELBO(q) = E_q[ log p(theta|D) + log P(D) ] - E_q[ log q(theta) ]
         = log P(D) + E_q[ log p(theta|D) - log q(theta) ]
         = log P(D) - KL( q(theta) || p(theta|D) )
```

Rearranged: **log P(D) - ELBO(q) = KL(q(theta) || p(theta|D))**, with no approximation in this last step. Since KL divergence is non-negative, this re-derives ELBO(q) <= log P(D), but it says more: the *gap* between the ELBO and the true log evidence is the KL divergence you wanted to minimize. Because log P(D) is a fixed number (a property of the data and the model, not of your choice of q), maximizing ELBO(q) over phi is **equivalent** to minimizing KL(q(theta) || p(theta|D)) over phi. You traded an intractable minimization (of a KL you can't evaluate) for a tractable maximization (of the ELBO, which you can).

sections.heading: The ELBO's Two-Term Decomposition: Reconstruction Minus KL-to-Prior
sections.body:
The ELBO as derived so far, E_q[log P(D,theta)] - E_q[log q(theta)], can be rewritten into a second, more practically useful form by factoring the joint P(D, theta) = P(D | theta) * P(theta) -- likelihood times prior, as in the first concept of this module:

```text
ELBO(q) = E_q[ log P(D|theta) + log P(theta) ] - E_q[ log q(theta) ]
         = E_q[ log P(D|theta) ] - ( E_q[ log q(theta) ] - E_q[ log P(theta) ] )
         = E_q[ log P(D|theta) ] - KL( q(theta) || P(theta) )
```

This two-term form is the one quoted most often, and each term has a clean interpretation. The first term, E_q[log P(D|theta)], is the expected log-likelihood of the observed data, averaged over samples of theta drawn from q. It rewards a q that puts its mass on values of theta under which the data is well explained, which is why it is called the **reconstruction term** (especially once the same formula appears inside a generative model, in the next section). The second term, KL(q(theta) || P(theta)), penalizes q for straying from the **prior**. It is a regularizer, pulling the approximate posterior back toward what you believed before seeing data and counterbalancing the first term's pull toward whatever best explains the data.

That trade-off is not a design choice bolted on afterward; it fell out of the Jensen's-inequality derivation with no extra assumptions. A q that fits the data extremely well but drifts far from the prior is penalized by the second term. A q that stays at the prior and ignores the data scores 0 on the second term but typically does poorly on the first. Maximizing the ELBO finds the balance, a Bayesian version of Occam's razor that comes from the math rather than being imposed by hand.

sections.heading: The Objective a Variational Autoencoder Is Trained to Maximize
sections.body:
A **Variational Autoencoder (VAE)** is variational inference applied to a specific generative model, with neural networks standing in for the distributions involved. The generative model assumes each observed data point x (an image, say) is produced from some latent variable z via a decoder network defining P(x | z), with a simple prior P(z) (almost always a standard Normal). The true posterior over the latent given the data, P(z | x), is intractable, like every posterior in this module, so a VAE trains an **encoder network** to output the parameters (mean and variance) of an approximate posterior q(z | x), a Gaussian conditioned on x. It plays the role q(theta) played throughout this concept, except that it is parameterized by a neural network instead of hand-set variational parameters.

The VAE's training loss is the negative of the two-term ELBO decomposition from the previous section, with D replaced by a single data point x and theta replaced by the latent z: **loss = -( E_q(z|x)[log P(x|z)] - KL(q(z|x) || P(z)) )**. The first term, the expected log-likelihood of x given a z sampled from the encoder's output distribution and passed through the decoder, is implemented as an ordinary **reconstruction loss**: pixel-wise cross-entropy (a Bernoulli decoder) or squared error (a Gaussian decoder with fixed variance) between the decoder's output and the input x. Squared error matches the negative log-likelihood only up to a scale factor and a constant, which is why many VAE implementations weight the two terms. The second term, the KL divergence between the encoder's output distribution and the prior over z, has a closed form when both are Gaussian (a formula in the encoder's predicted mean and variance) and acts as a regularizer that keeps the latent space close to the prior, rather than letting the encoder memorize each input as a narrow, disconnected spike. If you have covered KL divergence and cross-entropy as loss functions elsewhere in this curriculum, this is the connection: a VAE's loss is reconstruction cross-entropy plus a KL regularizer, because that sum is the negative ELBO, derived above from Jensen's inequality applied to the log evidence.

```python
import numpy as np

def vae_loss(x, x_reconstructed, mu, log_var):
    # Reconstruction term: negative log-likelihood, here as summed squared error,
    # which equals a Gaussian decoder's -log P(x|z) with variance 1/2, up to a constant.
    reconstruction_loss = np.sum((x - x_reconstructed) ** 2)

    # KL(q(z|x) || N(0, I)), closed form for two Gaussians -- the encoder's
    # output (mu, log_var) compared against the standard-normal prior.
    kl_term = -0.5 * np.sum(1 + log_var - mu ** 2 - np.exp(log_var))

    # ELBO = -reconstruction_loss - kl_term; the VAE MINIMIZES the negative ELBO,
    # which is this sum.
    return reconstruction_loss + kl_term
```

examples.title: The ELBO Is Never Larger Than the True Log Evidence
examples.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import quad
from scipy.stats import norm

# A toy 1D unnormalized posterior whose evidence we can also compute by brute
# force, so we can check the ELBO's guarantee numerically.
def unnormalized_posterior(theta):
    return np.exp(-0.5 * ((theta - 1.0) / 0.5) ** 2) + 0.3 * np.exp(-0.5 * ((theta + 2.0) / 1.5) ** 2)

true_evidence, _ = quad(unnormalized_posterior, -20, 20)
log_true_evidence = np.log(true_evidence)

def elbo(q_mean, q_std, n_samples=200000, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    z = rng.normal(q_mean, q_std, size=n_samples)
    log_p_joint = np.log(unnormalized_posterior(z))       # log P(D, theta), unnormalized
    log_q = norm.logpdf(z, q_mean, q_std)
    return np.mean(log_p_joint - log_q)                     # Monte Carlo estimate of E_q[...]

for q_mean, q_std in [(1.0, 0.5), (0.0, 2.0), (-1.0, 1.0)]:
    bound = elbo(q_mean, q_std)
    print(f"q=N({q_mean},{q_std})  ELBO={bound:.3f}  <=  log P(D)={log_true_evidence:.3f}")
# q=N(1.0,0.5)  ELBO=0.331  <=  log P(D)=0.868
# q=N(0.0,2.0)  ELBO=0.217  <=  log P(D)=0.868
# q=N(-1.0,1.0)  ELBO=0.139  <=  log P(D)=0.868
examples.explanation: Because this toy target's evidence can also be computed by brute force with `scipy.integrate.quad`, the example can check the ELBO's central guarantee: every ELBO printed (0.331, 0.217, 0.139) is below log_true_evidence (0.868), as Jensen's inequality requires, whichever Gaussian q is tried. The tightness varies. q=N(1.0, 0.5), which sits on the target's main mode, has the highest ELBO, and N(-1.0, 1.0), which sits between the two bumps, has the lowest. The gap between a q's ELBO and the log evidence is the KL divergence from that q to the true posterior, so the q with the largest ELBO of the three is the closest in KL(q || p), and you learn that without computing the KL. All three gaps are large (over 0.5 nats) because a single Gaussian cannot match this two-bump target well. The ELBO here is a Monte Carlo estimate, so values carry a little sampling noise.

examples.title: Fitting a Variational Approximation by Directly Maximizing the ELBO
examples.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize
from scipy.stats import norm

def unnormalized_posterior(theta):
    d1 = np.exp(-0.5 * ((theta - 2.0) / 0.6) ** 2)
    d2 = np.exp(-0.5 * ((theta + 1.5) / 0.6) ** 2)
    return 0.7 * d1 + 0.3 * d2                       # a bimodal target

def negative_elbo(params, n_samples=20000, seed=1):
    q_mean, log_q_std = params
    q_std = np.exp(log_q_std)                          # keep std positive during optimization
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    z = rng.normal(q_mean, q_std, size=n_samples)
    log_joint = np.log(unnormalized_posterior(z) + 1e-300)
    log_q = norm.logpdf(z, q_mean, q_std)
    return -np.mean(log_joint - log_q)                  # minimize negative ELBO = maximize ELBO

result = minimize(negative_elbo, x0=[0.0, 0.0], method="Nelder-Mead")
fitted_mean, fitted_log_std = result.x
print(f"best single-Gaussian fit: mean={fitted_mean:.3f}  std={np.exp(fitted_log_std):.3f}")
# best single-Gaussian fit: mean=2.000  std=0.613
examples.explanation: This is variational inference as the explanation describes it: instead of sampling from the bimodal target with MCMC, the code uses numerical optimization to find the single Gaussian q that maximizes the ELBO, which is the single Gaussian closest to the bimodal posterior in KL(q || p). The fit lands on the heavier mode (mean 2.000, the bump at 2.0 with weight 0.7, std 0.613 against the bump's 0.6) instead of spreading to cover both. A single Gaussian cannot represent two separated bumps, and KL(q || p) heavily penalizes putting q's mass where p is near zero, so the optimum captures one mode accurately rather than covering both poorly. (This mode-seeking behavior belongs to this direction of the KL; a Nelder-Mead start near the other mode can end up there, since each mode is a local optimum.) It shows the main limitation of VI: accuracy is capped by how expressive the chosen family is, not only by how well it is optimized.

examples.title: A Minimal VAE Loss: Reconstruction Minus KL, Made Concrete
examples.code:
import numpy as np

def encoder(x):
    # Stand-in for a real neural network: maps an input to (mu, log_var)
    # describing the approximate posterior q(z|x). Here a toy linear map.
    mu = 0.5 * x
    log_var = np.full_like(x, -1.0)
    return mu, log_var

def decoder(z):
    # Stand-in for a real neural network mapping a latent sample back to a
    # reconstruction of x.
    return 2.0 * z

def vae_loss(x):
    mu, log_var = encoder(x)
    std = np.exp(0.5 * log_var)
    eps = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=x.shape)     # the "reparameterization trick"
    z = mu + std * eps                                        # a differentiable sample from q(z|x)

    x_reconstructed = decoder(z)
    reconstruction_loss = np.sum((x - x_reconstructed) ** 2)
    kl_term = -0.5 * np.sum(1 + log_var - mu ** 2 - np.exp(log_var))

    return reconstruction_loss + kl_term    # this sum IS the negative ELBO

x = np.array([1.0, -2.0, 0.5])
print(vae_loss(x))   # 1.8605...
examples.explanation: Each line maps onto a term from the derivation: `encoder(x)` produces the variational parameters phi (here, mu and log_var) of q(z|x); `z = mu + std * eps` draws a sample from q(z|x) using the reparameterization trick, which rewrites sampling as a differentiable function of mu, std, and an independent noise source, so gradients can flow back through the sampling step during training; `reconstruction_loss` is the negative of E_q[log P(x|z)] (up to constants, for a Gaussian decoder), the ELBO's first term; `kl_term` is the closed-form KL(q(z|x) || N(0,I)), the ELBO's second term. Their sum is the negative ELBO (estimated from one sample of z), and minimizing it during training maximizes the ELBO. There is no additional VAE-specific loss; 'training a VAE' and 'maximizing the ELBO of this latent-variable model' are the same statement.

misconceptions.description: The ELBO is a heuristic or approximate loss that's merely 'inspired by' or 'analogous to' the true Bayesian objective, not rigorously tied to it.
misconceptions.clarification: The ELBO is derived from Jensen's inequality applied to the log marginal likelihood, and the gap between the ELBO and the true log evidence equals KL(q||p(theta|D)); it is not an approximation of that gap, it is the gap. Maximizing the ELBO over the variational parameters is therefore EQUIVALENT to minimizing that KL divergence, not merely correlated with it. The numerical example in this concept shows the ELBO never exceeding the true log evidence for any q tried, as the derivation predicts.
misconceptions.fact: The ELBO is derived from an application of Jensen's inequality to the log marginal likelihood, and the gap between the ELBO and the true log evidence is exactly equal to KL(q||p(theta|D)).

misconceptions.description: Because variational inference produces an explicit closed-form distribution q(theta) instead of raw samples, it always gives a more accurate picture of the true posterior than MCMC.
misconceptions.clarification: VI's accuracy is capped by the expressiveness of the variational family you chose. A mean-field Gaussian cannot represent multimodality or strong correlations between parameters, as the bimodal example shows (the fitted Gaussian sits on one mode instead of covering both). MCMC is asymptotically exact given enough samples and time, with no equivalent ceiling on the shapes it can represent. The trade-off is that VI is typically much faster and more scalable, at the cost of a bias set by the family, while MCMC is typically slower but free of that bias. An explicit formula does not mean a more accurate one.

exercises.prompt: This VAE loss function trains, but produces oddly blurry, generic-looking reconstructions no matter how long training runs, and the latent samples for very different inputs end up nearly identical. Find the bug relative to the correct ELBO decomposition and fix it.
exercises.code:
import numpy as np

def vae_loss(x, mu, log_var, x_reconstructed):
    reconstruction_loss = np.sum((x - x_reconstructed) ** 2)
    kl_term = -0.5 * np.sum(1 + log_var - mu ** 2 - np.exp(log_var))

    kl_weight = 50.0   # scales up the KL term relative to reconstruction
    return reconstruction_loss + kl_weight * kl_term
hints: Compare the two terms' relative sizes: reconstruction_loss is typically on the scale of pixel differences, while kl_term for a well-behaved encoder is often modest too, so multiplying kl_term by 50 makes the regularizer dominate the total loss.

If the KL term overwhelms the reconstruction term, the optimizer will happily push q(z|x) toward matching the prior for EVERY input, since that drives kl_term toward 0 regardless of how badly x is reconstructed -- which is the 'nearly identical latents for different inputs' symptom.

The ELBO's two terms are meant to be balanced by the math itself (reconstruction minus KL, both with implicit weight 1) -- introducing an extra multiplier like kl_weight=50 no longer maximizes the ELBO; it is a different, over-regularized objective.
exercises.solutionCode:
import numpy as np

def vae_loss(x, mu, log_var, x_reconstructed):
    reconstruction_loss = np.sum((x - x_reconstructed) ** 2)
    kl_term = -0.5 * np.sum(1 + log_var - mu ** 2 - np.exp(log_var))

    return reconstruction_loss + kl_term    # fixed: no extra weighting -- this IS the negative ELBO
exercises.solutionExplanation: The negative ELBO is reconstruction_loss + kl_term, with both terms at weight 1, because that sum falls out of the Jensen's-inequality derivation. Multiplying kl_term by 50 makes the objective something other than the ELBO: it over-penalizes any q(z|x) that drifts from the prior, so the easiest way to reduce the KL-dominated loss is to push every input's encoder output toward the prior regardless of x. That gives nearly identical latents for different inputs and blurry, generic decoder outputs, a failure mode known as posterior collapse. (Practitioners do sometimes use a KL weight on purpose, as in the beta-VAE, but then the objective is no longer the ELBO, and a weight of 50 is far beyond what the data scale justifies.) The fix removes the extra weight and restores the reconstruction-minus-KL balance.

exercises.prompt: Given these two candidate Gaussian approximations q1 and q2 for the same fixed unnormalized target, and their ELBO values already computed as elbo_q1 and elbo_q2 below, what does this print, and which q is closer to the true posterior in KL divergence?
exercises.code:
elbo_q1 = -12.4    # E_q1[log p_tilde(theta)] - E_q1[log q1(theta)]
elbo_q2 = -9.1     # E_q2[log p_tilde(theta)] - E_q2[log q2(theta)]
log_true_evidence = -8.0   # computed once, by brute-force numerical integration, for comparison

kl_q1 = log_true_evidence - elbo_q1
kl_q2 = log_true_evidence - elbo_q2

print(round(kl_q1, 2), round(kl_q2, 2))
print("q1 is closer" if kl_q1 < kl_q2 else "q2 is closer")
hints: Recall the identity from this concept: log P(D) - ELBO(q) = KL(q || p(theta|D)) -- so each KL value is just log_true_evidence minus that q's ELBO.
kl_q1 = -8.0 - (-12.4) = 4.4, and kl_q2 = -8.0 - (-9.1) = 1.1 -- compute both before looking at the comparison.
A SMALLER KL divergence means q is closer to the true posterior -- and a higher ELBO always corresponds to a smaller KL, since ELBO = log_true_evidence - KL.
exercises.expectedAnswer: It prints 4.4 1.1, then "q2 is closer". kl_q1 = -8.0 - (-12.4) = 4.4, kl_q2 = -8.0 - (-9.1) = 1.1, and since 1.1 < 4.4, q2 has the smaller KL divergence to the true posterior and is therefore the better approximation, consistent with q2 having the higher ELBO of the two.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Using the identity log P(D) - ELBO(q) = KL(q||p(theta|D)), kl_q1 is -8.0 minus -12.4, which is 4.4, and kl_q2 is -8.0 minus -9.1, which is 1.1. Since 1.1 is smaller than 4.4, q2 is the closer approximation in KL divergence. That ranking matches the ranking by raw ELBO (-9.1 is higher than -12.4), which is the practical payoff of the identity: you can rank candidate approximations, or track whether an optimizer is improving q, by watching the ELBO go up, without knowing log_true_evidence or computing any KL. The exercise computes the KL values only to make the identity concrete.

assessments.prompt: Jensen's inequality is used to derive the ELBO from log P(D) = log E_q[P(D,theta)/q(theta)]. What does Jensen's inequality guarantee here, and why does that make the ELBO a LOWER bound rather than an upper bound?
options: Jensen's inequality guarantees E[log X] >= log E[X] for any random variable X, which directly makes the ELBO an upper bound, not a lower bound -- the naming in this concept is a historical convention only, so the direction of the bound depends on which of the two quantities a given textbook chooses to write first.
Jensen's inequality applies only when q(theta) is chosen to exactly equal the true posterior, and guarantees equality (not an inequality) in every other case.

Because log is a concave function, Jensen's inequality guarantees log E_q[X] >= E_q[log X] for the positive quantity X = P(D,theta)/q(theta); applying that to log P(D) shows log P(D) is always at least as large as E_q[log X], i.e. the ELBO, making the ELBO a genuine lower bound on log P(D).
Jensen's inequality guarantees that the ELBO equals log P(D) minus a fixed constant that does not depend on q, so the two always differ by the same fixed amount.
assessments.explanation: The derivation above shows it: log is concave, so Jensen's inequality gives log E_q[X] >= E_q[log X], and setting X = P(D,theta)/q(theta) turns log P(D) itself into the left side of that inequality, with the ELBO as the right side -- proving log P(D) >= ELBO(q), i.e. the ELBO never exceeds the true log evidence, which is why it is called a lower bound. The “Jensen's inequality guarantees E[log X] >= log…” option states the inequality backwards (it's log E[X] >= E[log X], not the reverse) and draws the wrong conclusion from it. The “Jensen's inequality applies only when q(theta)…” option is false: the inequality holds for any q and is strict unless q equals the true posterior, which is the opposite of 'every other case.' The “Jensen's inequality guarantees that the ELBO equals…” option is false -- the gap between the ELBO and log P(D) is KL(q||p(theta|D)), which depends on q and shrinks as q improves; it is not a fixed constant.

assessments.prompt: A Variational Autoencoder's loss is reconstruction_loss + kl_term, minimized during training. Which statement correctly identifies what this loss is, in terms of this concept's derivation?
options: It is a Metropolis-Hastings acceptance ratio computed once per training example rather than once per MCMC step.

It is an ad-hoc loss combining two unrelated ideas -- an autoencoder's usual reconstruction loss, plus a regularizer borrowed from a different, unrelated area of statistics, so minimizing it has no probabilistic meaning beyond producing smooth reconstructions and a tidy latent space.
It is the marginal likelihood P(x), computed directly, with kl_term serving only as a numerical stabilization trick with no probabilistic meaning.

It is exactly the negative ELBO for the VAE's latent-variable model: reconstruction_loss is the negative of the expected-log-likelihood term E_q(z|x)[log P(x|z)], and kl_term is exactly KL(q(z|x) || P(z)), so minimizing their sum is exactly maximizing the ELBO.
assessments.explanation: The VAE's training loss is the negative of the two-term ELBO decomposition: the reconstruction loss corresponds to the negative expected log-likelihood term (up to constants for a squared-error decoder) and the KL term is KL(q(z|x)||P(z)). There is no separate VAE-specific objective. The “It is an ad-hoc loss combining two…” option is false: the two terms are two halves of one derivation (Jensen's inequality applied to the log evidence), not a reconstruction loss with an unrelated regularizer bolted on. The “It is the marginal likelihood P(x), computed…” option is false: P(x) is the intractable quantity the ELBO exists to avoid computing, and the loss is a bound on it, not the marginal likelihood itself. The “It is a Metropolis-Hastings acceptance ratio computed…” option confuses two different algorithms from this module; a VAE's loss involves no accept/reject step.

assessments.prompt: Explain, using Jensen's inequality and the exact identity log P(D) - ELBO(q) = KL(q||p(theta|D)), why maximizing the ELBO is equivalent to minimizing the KL divergence between the approximate and true posterior, and then explain how this same objective becomes the training loss of a Variational Autoencoder.
assessments.modelAnswer: Variational inference wants to minimize KL(q(theta)||p(theta|D)) over the variational parameters of q, but that KL divergence can't be computed directly, because p(theta|D) contains the intractable marginal likelihood P(D) in its denominator. The ELBO is derived by applying Jensen's inequality (log is concave, so log of an expectation is at least the expectation of the log) to log P(D) rewritten as log E_q[P(D,theta)/q(theta)], giving log P(D) >= E_q[log P(D,theta)] - E_q[log q(theta)], which defines the ELBO as this lower bound. This is more than an inequality, because the gap is known exactly: log P(D) - ELBO(q) equals KL(q(theta)||p(theta|D)), derivable by factoring P(D,theta) as p(theta|D)P(D) inside the ELBO's expectation. Since log P(D) is a fixed number that doesn't depend on q at all, that identity means increasing the ELBO by exactly some amount decreases the KL divergence by that exact same amount -- so maximizing the ELBO over q's parameters is the same optimization problem as minimizing the KL divergence, not merely correlated with it. This is the objective a Variational Autoencoder trains: it defines a decoder network specifying a generative model P(x|z)P(z), and an encoder network producing the parameters of an approximate posterior q(z|x) over the latent z given an observed x. The ELBO for this model decomposes into E_q(z|x)[log P(x|z)] (an expected log-likelihood, implemented in code as an ordinary reconstruction loss like pixel-wise cross-entropy or MSE) minus KL(q(z|x)||P(z)) (a closed-form KL divergence between the encoder's output and the prior, usually a standard Normal, acting as a regularizer on the latent space). A VAE's loss, reconstruction loss plus KL term, is the negative of this ELBO. Minimizing that sum maximizes the ELBO of its latent-variable model, which by the identity above trains the encoder to approximate the intractable posterior over the latent variable as closely as its Gaussian family allows.

concepts.title: Bayesian Networks, Markov Random Fields, and Factor Graphs
concepts.description: Bayesian Networks factorize a joint distribution over a directed acyclic graph of conditional-probability tables. Markov Random Fields do the undirected analogue with clique potentials and a partition function that is the same intractable normalizing quantity as the evidence. Factor graphs unify both into one bipartite representation whose message-passing inference algorithm is the conceptual ancestor of graph neural network message passing.
learningObjectives: Define a Bayesian Network as a directed acyclic graph encoding a factorization of the joint distribution into per-node conditional distributions given parents.
Explain how a Bayesian Network's DAG structure encodes conditional independence assumptions, and describe d-separation at an intuitive level.
Define a Markov Random Field as the undirected analogue built from potential functions over cliques and a partition function, and contrast its independence semantics with a Bayesian Network's.
Define a factor graph as a bipartite graph connecting variable nodes to factor nodes, and explain why it unifies and generalizes both directed and undirected representations.

Explain why explicit conditional-independence structure matters in practice (efficient inference via message passing, fewer parameters, interpretability) and describe the conceptual link between factor-graph message passing and graph neural network message passing.

sections.heading: Bayesian Networks: Factorizing the Joint via a DAG
sections.body:
Without any structural assumptions, a joint distribution over n discrete random variables, each taking one of k values, requires a table of k^n numbers to specify fully (k^n - 1 free parameters), which explodes so fast that even a few dozen variables make brute-force joint tables unworkable. A **Bayesian Network** avoids that by encoding a structured factorization. It is a **directed acyclic graph (DAG)** where each node is a random variable, and the joint distribution factorizes as the product, over every node, of that node's probability given only its **parents** in the graph: P(X_1, ..., X_n) = product over i of P(X_i | parents(X_i)). Each node stores only a **conditional probability table (CPT)** relating it to its own parents, not to every other variable in the model, and that is where the savings come from.

Take a tiny medical model with a disease D and two symptoms S1 and S2, with edges D -> S1 and D -> S2 (the disease causes each symptom, and given the disease the symptoms are unrelated). The joint P(D, S1, S2) factorizes as P(D) * P(S1|D) * P(S2|D): three small tables instead of one joint table over every combination of all three variables. The factorization is more than a computational convenience; it *is* a set of conditional independence claims, spelled out in the next section. Querying it, for instance computing P(D | S1=observed), is an application of Bayes' theorem from the first concept of this module, now inside a larger structured joint rather than on a single parameter.

```python
import itertools

# Tiny hand-built CPTs for D -> S1, D -> S2
p_d = {True: 0.01, False: 0.99}                                  # P(disease)
p_s1_given_d = {True: {True: 0.9, False: 0.1}, False: {True: 0.05, False: 0.95}}
p_s2_given_d = {True: {True: 0.8, False: 0.2}, False: {True: 0.1, False: 0.9}}

def joint(d, s1, s2):
    return p_d[d] * p_s1_given_d[d][s1] * p_s2_given_d[d][s2]

# Query P(D=True | S1=True) by brute-force enumeration: sum out S2, normalize over D
numerator = sum(joint(True, True, s2) for s2 in (True, False))
evidence = sum(joint(d, True, s2) for d in (True, False) for s2 in (True, False))
print(round(numerator / evidence, 4))   # 0.1538: posterior probability of disease given symptom 1

sections.heading: Conditional Independence and D-Separation
sections.body:
The graph in a Bayesian Network is not just a diagram of which variables 'relate' to which; it licenses checkable conditional independence claims. The **local Markov property** states that every node is conditionally independent of its non-descendants, given its parents. In the disease example, S1 and S2 are conditionally independent given D: once you know whether the disease is present, learning the value of S1 tells you nothing further about S2. All of the dependence between the two symptoms flows *through* the shared cause D, and conditioning on D blocks that flow.

The general rule for reading conditional independence off any DAG, including cases much less obvious than a single shared parent, is **d-separation**: two variables are independent given a conditioning set if every path between them is 'blocked' by that set, according to a few rules about how local graph patterns behave. Two patterns are worth knowing by name because they behave in opposite, easily confused ways. A **common cause** (two effects of one cause, like S1 and S2 given D) makes the two effects dependent in general, but conditionally independent once you observe the cause, as above. A **collider** (two independent causes of a shared effect, such as two risk factors that both influence one observed outcome) behaves the other way: the causes are independent in general, but conditioning on the shared effect can make them dependent. This counter-intuitive effect is called **explaining away**: once you know the effect occurred, learning that one cause is present makes the other cause *less* likely, creating a dependence between variables that were unrelated beforehand.

The explaining-away effect is easy to check by enumeration. Take a burglary B (probability 0.01) and an earthquake E (probability 0.02), independent causes of an alarm A, with P(A | B, E) = 0.95, 0.94 for B only, 0.29 for E only, and 0.001 for neither:

```python
from itertools import product

p_b, p_e = 0.01, 0.02                     # two independent causes
p_a = {(1, 1): 0.95, (1, 0): 0.94, (0, 1): 0.29, (0, 0): 0.001}   # P(alarm | B, E)

def joint(b, e, a):
    pb = p_b if b else 1 - p_b
    pe = p_e if e else 1 - p_e
    pa = p_a[(b, e)] if a else 1 - p_a[(b, e)]
    return pb * pe * pa

def prob_b(**ev):                          # P(B=1 | evidence) by enumeration
    num = den = 0.0
    for b, e, a in product((0, 1), repeat=3):
        if any({"e": e, "a": a}[k] != v for k, v in ev.items()):
            continue
        den += joint(b, e, a)
        num += joint(b, e, a) * b
    return num / den

print(round(prob_b(), 4))                  # 0.01    prior P(B)
print(round(prob_b(e=1), 4))               # 0.01    earthquake alone says nothing about B
print(round(prob_b(a=1), 4))               # 0.5835  alarm observed
print(round(prob_b(a=1, e=1), 4))          # 0.032   alarm, and the earthquake is known
```

The alarm raises the burglary probability from 0.01 to 0.58. Learning that an earthquake happened drops it to 0.032, because the earthquake now explains the alarm. B and E are independent until A is observed.

The payoff of taking this structure seriously is threefold: **fewer parameters** to estimate from data (a handful of small CPTs instead of one exponentially large joint table), **interpretability** (the edges are an inspectable claim about which dependencies the model believes exist, not an opaque black box), and **efficient inference** (algorithms that exploit the graph's structure, like variable elimination and belief propagation, avoid materializing the full joint distribution, which is intractable for any nontrivial number of variables). A dense, unstructured joint distribution offers none of the three.

sections.heading: Markov Random Fields: The Undirected Analogue
sections.body:
A **Markov Random Field (MRF)** drops both the directionality and the acyclicity requirement of a Bayesian Network. It replaces the DAG-plus-CPTs factorization with an undirected graph and a different building block: **potential functions** psi_c(x_c), one for each **clique** c (a fully-connected subset of variables) in the graph, which assign a non-negative 'compatibility score' to every combination of values the variables in that clique could take. psi_c is *not* a probability distribution on its own; it is a scoring function. The joint distribution is the product of every clique's potential, divided by a single global normalizing constant Z: p(x) = (1/Z) * product over cliques c of psi_c(x_c), where Z = sum (or integral) over every possible joint configuration of x of that same product.

Z is the **partition function**, and it plays the role the marginal likelihood P(D) played in the first concept of this module: a single normalizing constant, defined by summing over an (astronomically large) configuration space, generally without a closed form once the graph has more than a handful of variables. Computing Z exactly is in general as intractable as computing the evidence, for the same reason: it requires summing over exponentially many joint configurations.

MRFs have simpler independence semantics: two sets of variables are conditionally independent given a third set if removing the third set from the graph disconnects the first two. This purely topological criterion has none of d-separation's collider subtleties, because there is no edge direction to reason about. A minimal example is a three-node undirected chain A - B - C with pairwise potentials psi(A,B) and psi(B,C), where the normalized joint requires summing the product of both potentials over every combination of A, B, and C. This is the setting Gibbs sampling, from the previous concept, was developed for. When Z can't be computed, sampling from the unnormalized potentials via MCMC is the practical route to inference, the same evidence-avoidance trick from earlier in this module, applied to an MRF's partition function instead of a posterior's marginal likelihood.

```python
import itertools

# A tiny 3-node MRF chain A - B - C with hand-set pairwise potentials.
def psi_ab(a, b):
    return 2.0 if a == b else 0.5     # "compatibility": A and B prefer to agree

def psi_bc(b, c):
    return 1.5 if b == c else 0.7

states = list(itertools.product([0, 1], repeat=3))   # every (A, B, C) combination
unnormalized = {s: psi_ab(s[0], s[1]) * psi_bc(s[1], s[2]) for s in states}

Z = sum(unnormalized.values())                          # the partition function
normalized = {s: v / Z for s, v in unnormalized.items()}

print("Z =", Z)                                         # 11.0 (2 * 2.5 * 2.2: sum over B of the two row sums)
print(sum(normalized.values()))                          # 1.0, as required
# Note: enumerating all 2^3 = 8 states was easy here -- for 100 binary variables
# it would require summing over 2^100 states, which is why Z is generally intractable.

sections.heading: Factor Graphs: One Representation for Both, and the Bridge to Graph Neural Networks
sections.body:
A **factor graph** makes the factorization an explicit part of the graph, rather than leaving it implicit in a DAG's CPTs or an MRF's cliques. It is a **bipartite graph** with two kinds of nodes: **variable nodes** (one per random variable) and **factor nodes** (one per term in the factorization: one per CPT in a Bayesian Network, or one per clique potential in an MRF), with an edge connecting each factor node to every variable node it depends on. The joint distribution is the product of every factor node's function, evaluated at the variables it is connected to (divided by a normalizing constant if the factors aren't already normalized). Both representations covered above translate directly into this one: a Bayesian Network's CPT P(X_i | parents(X_i)) becomes one factor node connected to X_i and each of its parents; an MRF's clique potential psi_c(x_c) becomes one factor node connected to every variable in that clique. That is why factor graphs are often treated as the unifying representation: both of the others translate into one.

The main practical payoff of making the factorization explicit is that exact inference gets a local description. The **sum-product algorithm** (belief propagation) computes marginal distributions by passing **messages** along the edges of the graph. Each message is a function, sent from one node to a neighbor, summarizing what the sender believes about the shared variable based on what it has heard from its *other* neighbors. A node's outgoing message is computed from its local factor (or, for a variable node, by combining its incoming messages) and the messages it has received; no node needs to see the whole graph. On a tree-structured factor graph, running this procedure (two sweeps, or iterating until messages stop changing) yields the *exact* marginal at every variable node, at a cost that scales with the size of the graph instead of exploding combinatorially like brute-force enumeration. On graphs with loops the same updates are only an approximation (loopy belief propagation) and may not converge.

This is also the most direct bridge to modern deep learning. A **Graph Neural Network's** message-passing layer follows the same template as belief propagation, generalized and made learnable. Each node aggregates messages from its neighbors, computed by some function of the neighbor's current representation and the connecting edge, and updates its own representation. That mirrors belief propagation's 'gather from neighbors, combine, send updated summaries onward' pattern, except that a GNN's messages are learned, differentiable vectors optimized end to end rather than hand-derived probabilistic summaries. **Structured prediction** (jointly predicting a whole sequence of labels rather than one label at a time) is the classical setting that motivated much of this machinery well before GNNs. A **Conditional Random Field (CRF)**, an MRF (equivalently, a factor graph) over a label sequence conditioned on an input, is the standard example. Seeing factor graphs and message passing here is a good route to understanding why a GNN's message-passing layer has the shape it does.

examples.title: Exact Inference in a Tiny Bayesian Network by Enumeration
examples.explanation: Observing both symptoms raises the posterior probability of disease from 0.1538 to 0.5926, which the factorization P(D)P(S1|D)P(S2|D) predicts: because S1 and S2 are conditionally independent given D, each observed symptom multiplies in its own likelihood factor P(S_i|D), compounding the evidence for D instead of being redundant with the first. (The prior odds of 1:99 are multiplied by 0.9/0.05 = 18 for S1 and again by 0.8/0.1 = 8 for S2, giving odds of about 1.45:1.) The computation, summing out unobserved variables in the numerator and summing over all values of D in the denominator, is the likelihood-times-prior-over-evidence structure from the first concept, applied inside a graph with several variables.

examples.title: A Markov Random Field's Partition Function, and Why It Explodes
examples.code:
import itertools
import time

def psi_pairwise(a, b, agree_bonus=2.0):
    return agree_bonus if a == b else 1.0

def partition_function(n_nodes):
    # A chain of n_nodes binary variables, each adjacent pair sharing a potential.
    total = 0.0
    for state in itertools.product([0, 1], repeat=n_nodes):
        value = 1.0
        for i in range(n_nodes - 1):
            value *= psi_pairwise(state[i], state[i + 1])
        total += value
    return total

for n in [4, 8, 16, 20]:
    start = time.time()
    z = partition_function(n)
    print(f"n={n:>2}  states_enumerated={2**n:>10}  Z={z:.2f}  time={time.time()-start:.4f}s")
examples.explanation: Every additional node doubles the number of states that must be enumerated to compute Z, so the runtime grows exponentially even for this simple chain-structured MRF. By n=20 the code is summing over a million states, and a graph of realistic size (hundreds of variables, or a dense structure rather than a chain) makes brute-force enumeration infeasible. For this chain Z has the closed form 2 * 3^(n-1) (54 for n=4, 4374 for n=8), because each added node multiplies the sum by 1 + 2 = 3. Dynamic programming, closely related to the message passing in the factor-graph section, computes Z for any chain in time linear in n. For a general densely connected MRF no such trick exists, which is why MCMC methods like Gibbs sampling were developed in this very setting.

examples.title: Sum-Product Message Passing on a Small Chain
examples.code:
import numpy as np

# A 3-variable chain X1 -- X2 -- X3, each binary, with pairwise factors.
# factor[i] gives compatibility between X_i and X_{i+1} as a 2x2 matrix.
factor_12 = np.array([[2.0, 0.5], [0.5, 2.0]])
factor_23 = np.array([[1.0, 1.0], [1.0, 3.0]])

# Message from X1 to X2: for each value of X2, sum over X1's values,
# weighted by the factor connecting them (X1 has no other neighbors, so no
# incoming message to combine with -- this is the "forward pass" base case).
msg_1_to_2 = factor_12.sum(axis=0)               # shape (2,): [sum over x1 of factor_12[x1, x2=0], ... x2=1]
print("message X1->X2:", msg_1_to_2)   # [2.5 2.5]

# Message from X2 to X3: for each value of X3, sum over X2's values,
# weighted by factor_23 AND by whatever X2 already heard from X1.
msg_2_to_3 = (factor_23 * msg_1_to_2[:, None]).sum(axis=0)
print("message X2->X3:", msg_2_to_3)   # [ 5. 10.]

# The (unnormalized) marginal belief at X3 is this incoming message.
belief_x3 = msg_2_to_3 / msg_2_to_3.sum()
print("normalized marginal belief at X3:", belief_x3)   # [0.333 0.667]
examples.explanation: Each message is a summary, sent along one edge of the graph, of everything 'upstream' of that edge, computed by combining a local factor with the messages that have already arrived. `msg_1_to_2` summarizes X1's influence on X2, with nothing else needed since X1 has no other neighbors. `msg_2_to_3` folds that message together with factor_23 before summing out X2, propagating X1's influence to X3 without building the full three-variable joint table. This chain is small enough to check by enumerating all 8 (X1,X2,X3) combinations: the unnormalized marginal of X3 is [5, 10] both ways. Message passing is not an approximation here but an exact, cheaper reorganization of the same sum, which is why sum-product gives exact marginals on tree-structured graphs like this one. Note that no factor was normalized in this example, so only the final normalized belief is a probability.

misconceptions.description: An edge in a Bayesian Network represents a direct causal relationship between the two variables it connects.
misconceptions.clarification: A DAG edge represents a claimed direct probabilistic dependence in the chosen factorization. It is consistent with causation, but not proof of it. The same joint distribution can often be encoded by more than one DAG with different edge directions (Markov-equivalent DAGs imply the same conditional independence statements), so observational data and conditional-independence testing alone cannot establish which direction, if any, is causal without further causal assumptions or interventional data. The graph encodes a factorization of a probability distribution; a causal interpretation is a separate claim laid on top of it.
misconceptions.fact: A DAG edge represents a claimed direct probabilistic dependence used in the chosen factorization; it is consistent with causation but not proof of it.

misconceptions.description: Because Markov Random Fields use undirected edges instead of directed ones, they are strictly weaker or less expressive than Bayesian Networks.
misconceptions.clarification: Bayesian Networks and Markov Random Fields are different, not strictly ordered by expressive power. Some conditional independence structures can be represented exactly by an MRF but by no DAG (for example, a four-node cycle), and vice versa (a DAG's collider pattern has no exact undirected equivalent). Directionality determines the independence semantics, d-separation's asymmetric rules versus an MRF's topological separation, not how complex the interactions within a clique can be: a potential over a large clique can encode arbitrarily intricate joint interactions among its variables.

exercises.prompt: Given this Bayesian Network's CPTs (a Rain node causing a Sprinkler-off tendency, both causing Wet Grass), what does this print for P(Rain=True | WetGrass=True)?
hints: The numerator sums out the sprinkler variable while holding Rain=True and WetGrass=True fixed -- compute joint(True, True, True) and joint(True, False, True) and add them.
The evidence sums over every combination of Rain and Sprinkler while holding WetGrass=True fixed -- that is four joint(...) terms in total, including the two you computed for the numerator.
This is the likelihood-times-prior-over-evidence structure from the first concept, with the 'evidence' now summed over two variables (Rain and Sprinkler) jointly.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 0.3849 -- joint(True,True,True)=0.2*0.01*0.99=0.00198 and joint(True,False,True)=0.2*0.99*0.9=0.1782 sum to a numerator of 0.18018; adding joint(False,True,True)=0.8*0.4*0.9=0.288 and joint(False,False,True)=0.8*0.6*0.0=0.0 gives an evidence of 0.46818; 0.18018/0.46818 rounds to 0.3849.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Computing each term: joint(True,True,True) = 0.2*0.01*0.99 = 0.00198; joint(True,False,True) = 0.2*0.99*0.9 = 0.1782; these sum to a numerator of 0.18018. For the evidence, also add joint(False,True,True) = 0.8*0.4*0.9 = 0.288 and joint(False,False,True) = 0.8*0.6*0.0 = 0.0, giving evidence = 0.18018 + 0.288 + 0.0 = 0.46818. The final ratio is 0.18018 / 0.46818 ≈ 0.3849. This is the classic 'wet grass' query: observing wet grass raises the probability of rain from its 0.2 prior to 0.385, because rain makes wet grass very likely (0.9 even with the sprinkler off), while the rival explanation, a sprinkler running on a dry day, has a joint probability of only 0.8 * 0.4 = 0.32 (0.288 once multiplied by the 0.9 wetting probability). The mechanism is the numerator-over-evidence enumeration used throughout this concept, with the sprinkler as one extra variable to sum out.

exercises.prompt: This function is supposed to return a properly normalized joint distribution over a small MRF's states, but a caller reports that summing the returned values doesn't give 1.0. Find and fix the bug.
hints: A Markov Random Field's joint distribution is (1/Z) times the product of clique potentials -- the function computes the product of potentials but never computes or divides by Z.
Z, the partition function, is the sum of the unnormalized values across every possible state -- compute that sum first, then divide every value by it.
The fix adds two lines: sum `unnormalized.values()` to get Z, then build a new dict dividing every value by Z, and return THAT instead of the raw unnormalized dict.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The function computed the product of clique potentials for every state correctly, but an MRF's joint distribution is that product divided by Z, the partition function, and the buggy version returned the raw products, which sum to Z = 11.0 instead of 1. The fix is the missing step: sum the unnormalized values across every state to get Z, then divide each by Z. This is an easy bug to introduce with MRFs. A Bayesian Network's CPTs are normalized locally, node by node, so their product is automatically a valid joint, but an MRF's potentials carry no such guarantee. Normalization has to happen once, globally, via Z, and it is easy to forget when translating the math into code.

assessments.prompt: What does a Bayesian Network's DAG structure and factorization P(X_1,...,X_n) = product of P(X_i | parents(X_i)) represent?
options: A definitive claim about which variables cause which other variables in the real world.
A set of conditional independence assumptions -- each variable is independent of its non-descendants given its parents.
A requirement that the graph must be fully connected, since otherwise no valid joint distribution can be defined.
A guarantee that every pair of connected variables is correlated more strongly than every pair of unconnected variables.
assessments.explanation: The factorization is a set of conditional independence claims (the local Markov property), which is what lets a handful of small conditional probability tables replace an exponentially large joint table. The “A definitive claim about which variables cause…” option overstates the claim: edges license dependence claims within the chosen factorization, not proof of real-world causation. The “A guarantee that every pair of connected…” option is false: a DAG says nothing about the magnitude of any dependence, only about which conditional independencies are assumed. The “A requirement that the graph must…” option is false: the example networks in this concept are sparse, not fully connected, and sparsity is the point of using a Bayesian Network.

assessments.prompt: The partition function Z in a Markov Random Field's joint distribution p(x) = (1/Z) * product of clique potentials is described as generally just as intractable as the marginal likelihood from earlier in this module. Why?
options: Because Z requires summing (or integrating) the product of all clique potentials over every possible joint configuration of the variables, a set of configurations that grows exponentially with the number of variables, mirroring why the evidence integral over a continuous parameter space is generally intractable.
Because clique potentials, unlike conditional probability tables, are not allowed to contain any numeric values greater than 1.
Because Z can only be computed if the MRF has exactly three variables, as in this concept's worked chain example.
Because Z is only needed when using Gibbs sampling, and is never needed for exact inference.
assessments.explanation: Both Z and the marginal likelihood P(D) are single normalizing constants obtained by summing or integrating over an entire configuration or parameter space, and both become infeasible once that space is large. The chain-MRF example shows the number of enumerated states doubling with every added variable. The “Because Z can only be computed…” option is false: the three-variable example was chosen for illustration, and the same definition of Z applies to MRFs of any size. The “Because clique potentials, unlike conditional probability tables…” option invents a constraint: clique potentials need only be non-negative, with no upper bound of 1. The “Because Z is only needed when using…” option is false: Z is needed for any exact computation of the normalized joint, and Gibbs sampling is one way to avoid needing it.

assessments.prompt: How does this concept describe the relationship between factor-graph message passing (the sum-product algorithm) and graph neural network message passing?
options: Factor graphs and GNNs both require the underlying graph to be fully connected in order to function at all.

A GNN's message-passing layer follows the same local, neighbor-aggregation template as belief propagation on a factor graph, but replaces the hand-derived probabilistic messages with learned, differentiable, real-valued vector messages optimized end-to-end.
They are unrelated techniques that happen to share the word 'message' by coincidence.
Graph neural networks were developed first, and belief propagation on factor graphs was later designed to imitate them.
assessments.explanation: GNN message passing generalizes belief propagation's 'gather from neighbors, combine, send updated summaries onward' pattern, with the difference that a GNN's messages are learned vectors rather than hand-derived probability summaries. The “They are unrelated techniques that happen…” option dismisses a structural connection as coincidental wording. The “Graph neural networks were developed first…” option reverses the chronology: factor graphs and belief propagation are the older machinery that structured prediction relied on before GNNs existed. The “Factor graphs and GNNs both require…” option is false: the chain example here is sparse, and message passing works because it exploits sparse, local graph structure.

assessments.prompt: Explain what problem factor graphs solve relative to Bayesian Networks and Markov Random Fields individually, and describe the conceptual link between the sum-product message-passing algorithm and how a modern graph neural network's message-passing layer works.
assessments.modelAnswer: Bayesian Networks and Markov Random Fields each factorize a joint distribution using structure, but they use two different building blocks (a Bayesian Network's per-node conditional probability tables given parents, and an MRF's per-clique potential functions), and each has different independence semantics (d-separation with its collider/explaining-away asymmetry for the directed case, purely topological separation for the undirected case). A factor graph unifies both into one representation by making the factorization itself an explicit part of the graph: a bipartite structure with variable nodes and factor nodes, where each factor node connects to exactly the variables it depends on, and the joint is the product of every factor's function over its connected variables. A Bayesian Network's CPTs and an MRF's clique potentials both translate directly into factor nodes, so both become special cases of one shared representation, and this uniformity lets a single inference algorithm, sum-product or belief propagation, apply to either kind of model without modification. Belief propagation computes exact marginal distributions, on tree-structured graphs, by passing messages along the graph's edges: each message is a function summarizing what one node currently believes about a shared variable, computed purely from its own local factor and whatever messages it has already received from its other neighbors, with no node ever needing global knowledge of the whole graph. This same template (local computation at each node, combined from messages sent by neighbors, propagated along graph edges) is what a graph neural network's message-passing layer generalizes: instead of hand-derived probabilistic summaries, a GNN's messages are learned, differentiable, real-valued vectors, and instead of converging to exact probabilistic marginals via a fixed algorithm, the whole process is trained end-to-end to produce useful node representations for whatever downstream task the network is optimized for. Factor graphs and belief propagation help explain why GNN message-passing layers have the shape they do: the classical probabilistic version came first, and the deep-learning version keeps its skeleton while replacing its internals with learned functions.
